coffee-scene:La Cafeotheque.name: La Caféothèque
coffee-scene:La Cafeotheque.teaser: Paris's first specialty roaster, a block off the Seine, with the sacks and the drum in the next room
coffee-scene:La Cafeotheque.story: In 2005, when a Paris coffee meant a bitter little shot of robusta at the zinc, Gloria Montenegro, a former Guatemalan ambassador to France, opened a roastery-café on the rue de l'Hôtel de Ville. She roasted on site, sold only single origins, never blends, and ran a coffee school in the back; several of the baristas and roasters who built the city's later scene learned there. It still rambles through a warren of small rooms with worn armchairs, a board of thirty-odd origins, and the smell of the roaster drifting in from the side. Calm, unhurried, and a short walk from the Île Saint-Louis.
coffee-scene:La Cafeotheque.why: Ask what came out of the roaster this week and drink it as a filter; take a bag of the same beans home.
facts: 52 rue de l'Hôtel de Ville, 4th (métro Saint-Paul)
Daily from about 9:00 to early evening; listings differ on the closing hour, so check
A single-origin filter or espresso, and beans to take away
For an hour with a book; the armchairs suit reading more than a laptop session, and it closes before dinner

sources.label: The Way to Coffee: La Caféothèque

coffee-scene:Belleville Brulerie.name: Belleville Brûlerie
coffee-scene:Belleville Brulerie.teaser: The 2013 micro-roastery whose beans now fill the hoppers of half the city's good cafés
coffee-scene:Belleville Brulerie.story: Three coffee people, Thomas Lehoux, David Flynn and Anselme Blayney, set up a small roaster in Belleville in 2013 with one idea: Paris would never drink well while its cafés bought beans from the big industrial houses. They roasted light, bought by farm and lot, and sold to any café owner willing to retrain the staff. Within a few years their bags were behind the counter at a long list of the new places, and Belleville Brûlerie became the beans most people mean when they say Paris coffee got good. It is a roastery first: you meet the coffee in other people's cups, or buy it by the bag.
coffee-scene:Belleville Brulerie.why: If you have a machine on board, this is the bag to buy in Paris: roasted here, a few days old.
facts: A bag of beans for home or the galley; in cafés, ask whose coffee is in the grinder
No: a roastery, not a café room. Ten Belles has its own card for the cup

coffee-scene:Telescope.name: Télescope
coffee-scene:Telescope.teaser: A tiny white room behind the Palais-Royal that showed the Right Bank what an espresso could taste like
coffee-scene:Telescope.story: Nicolas Clerc opened Télescope on the short rue Villedo in 2012, a few steps from the Palais-Royal garden, when the specialty idea was still a rumour in Paris. The room is barely bigger than its counter: white walls, a handful of seats, a big window, a slab of cake, and coffee made with obsessive care. It has never needed to grow. Le Fooding and Paris by Mouth listed it early, and it remains the kind of place where the barista will tell you the farm, the variety and why today's espresso is pulling short.
coffee-scene:Telescope.why: Come on a weekday morning, take the espresso at the counter, then walk it off in the Palais-Royal garden.
facts: Weekdays from about 8:30 into the afternoon; weekend opening varies between listings, so check
Espresso or a filter, with whatever cake is on the counter
No: a handful of seats, built for a cup and a conversation

linger:Salle Ovale, BnF Richelieu.name: Salle Ovale, BnF Richelieu
linger:Salle Ovale, BnF Richelieu.teaser: Under a glass dome, 160 seats and 20,000 open books, free to anyone who walks in
linger:Salle Ovale, BnF Richelieu.story: The oval reading room of the old Bibliothèque nationale took nearly forty years to finish, begun in 1897 and opened in 1936, and for most of its life it was for accredited researchers only. Since the Richelieu site reopened after its long restoration, it is open to everyone, with no card and no age limit. You come in from rue Vivienne into a huge pale hall ringed by bookcases, with the glazed dome far overhead, the names of cities in gold around the cornice, and about 20,000 volumes on the shelves: art history, heritage, digital arts, children's books and a deep run of bandes dessinées. The sound is pages turning.
linger:Salle Ovale, BnF Richelieu.why: Take a seat at the long tables on a Tuesday, when it stays open until 20:00, and work under the dome until dusk.
facts: Tuesday 10:00–20:00, Wednesday to Sunday 10:00–18:00; closed Monday (Oct 2026)
Nothing: there is no café in the room, so bring water and eat outside in the Jardin Vivienne
Yes: free, open access, long tables, and you can stay until closing

linger:Bibliothèque Mazarine.name: Bibliothèque Mazarine
linger:Bibliothèque Mazarine.teaser: France's oldest public library, still a working reading room under Mazarin's carved bookcases
linger:Bibliothèque Mazarine.story: Cardinal Mazarin opened his private library to scholars in 1643, which makes the Mazarine the oldest public library in France. It now sits inside the Institut de France on the Seine, and its long reading hall, with dark carved shelves running to the ceiling, marble busts and the river light from the tall windows, is still used every day for real work, not shown off as a museum. About 140 seats, no lending: everything is read on the spot. The quiet is the deep, scholarly kind, broken by the creak of the parquet and the occasional fetching of a seventeenth-century folio.
linger:Bibliothèque Mazarine.why: Ask for the free short pass with your ID and spend a morning writing in the room Mazarin built for readers.
facts: Weekdays 10:00–18:00, with Saturdays outside summer according to some listings; closed 1–15 August (seen Jul 2026); check before going
Nothing to order: show ID for a free pass of five consecutive days, once a year; an annual card is €15 (Oct 2026)
Yes, in silence: no calls, no snacks, a seat at a reading desk

linger:Anticafé.name: Anticafé
linger:Anticafé.teaser: You pay for the hours, not the cup: coffee, snacks and Wi-Fi included, and a seat you are meant to keep
linger:Anticafé.story: Paris cafés have an unspoken rule about laptops and one espresso stretched over an afternoon. Anticafé turned that rule inside out: you check in, the clock starts, and the coffee, tea, cold drinks and snacks are included in the hourly rate, with a cap for the full day. The rooms are set up like a shared living room, with big tables, sofas, power sockets, a small library and board games for the breaks. Several branches are spread across the city, including one by the Louvre and one at République, and groups can book a corner ahead.
linger:Anticafé.why: When you need a full working day in the centre without a café owner watching your cup, this is the honest deal.
facts: Several branches, including Louvre and République
Daytime into the evening; hours vary by branch
Unlimited coffee, tea and snacks, included in the time; about €6 an hour, capped near €26 a day at the Louvre branch (Oct 2026; was €5 and €24, seen Jul 2026)
Yes: that is the whole point. Book ahead for four or more

linger:Café de Flore.name: Café de Flore
linger:Café de Flore.teaser: Red banquettes and mirrors from the 1880s, and the upstairs room where Baldwin wrote over cognac
linger:Café de Flore.story: During the cold winters of the Occupation, Sartre and Beauvoir worked at the Flore because it had a stove and they had none; they arrived at opening and stayed all day. A few years later James Baldwin sat upstairs writing much of Go Tell It on the Mountain. The room has been kept as it was on purpose: red moleskine banquettes, mahogany, mirrors, white-aproned waiters carrying silver trays. The terrace is the stage, crowded and photographed. The first floor is where the café still behaves like a place to think, quieter, with the boulevard reduced to a murmur below.
linger:Café de Flore.why: Go up to the first floor in mid-afternoon, order one thing, and stay as long as you like.
facts: A hot chocolate or a glass of wine; expect to pay several times a neighbourhood café's price
With a notebook, upstairs; laptops sit awkwardly here

linger:Les Deux Magots.name: Les Deux Magots
linger:Les Deux Magots.teaser: Two carved Chinese figures on a pillar, a terrace facing the oldest church in Paris, jazz on Thursdays
linger:Les Deux Magots.story: Les Deux Magots has traded as a café since 1884, and it takes its name from the pair of carved, robed Chinese figures, the magots, that sit high on a pillar in the main room and look down over everyone. Hemingway and the Surrealists drank here; Flore next door, the old rival, claims the same crowd. The reason to come now is the view: the terrace faces the Romanesque bell tower of Saint-Germain-des-Prés across the little square, and the waiters will let one drink last an hour. On Thursday evenings a jazz group plays inside.
linger:Les Deux Magots.why: Take a terrace table facing the church at the end of the afternoon; the Saint-Germain quarter card covers the streets around.
facts: One drink, slowly; a coffee is about €7 (Oct 2026, from a recent listing)
No: this is a terrace for watching, not a desk

linger:Le Select.name: Le Sélect
linger:Le Select.teaser: The 1923 Montparnasse café that still serves past midnight, marble tables and all
linger:Le Select.story: Le Sélect opened on the boulevard du Montparnasse in 1923, when the crossroads at Vavin was the busiest painters' and writers' corner in the world, and for years it never closed at night. Hemingway sent the characters of The Sun Also Rises there; painters and poets drifted between it, the Dôme, the Rotonde and La Coupole across the road. It has stayed a working brasserie rather than a shrine: black-and-white waiters, the long zinc, marble tables, regulars reading the paper, and a crowd that thickens after the cinemas let out. It is the one of the four that still feels like the neighbourhood's own.
linger:Le Select.why: Come late, after dinner at La Coupole (its own card is in the tables), for a nightcap at the zinc.
facts: Daily from about 7:00 to 2:00, later on Friday and Saturday; listings disagree on the weekend closing hour
A beer or a glass of wine at the zinc, or a croque at any hour
With a paperback, yes; with a laptop, only in the quiet of mid-afternoon

linger:Le Pavillon des Canaux.name: Le Pavillon des Canaux
linger:Le Pavillon des Canaux.teaser: A canal keeper's house turned café: work in a former bedroom, or in the bathtub, with the water outside
linger:Le Pavillon des Canaux.story: The little house on the Bassin de la Villette once belonged to the canal service; in 2014 it was turned into a café where every room kept its domestic shape. You can take your coffee to a former bedroom, a sitting room with mismatched sofas, a kitchen table, or the bathroom, where the bathtub has been fitted with cushions for one person and a laptop. Downstairs serves lunch and weekend brunch; outside, the terrace looks over the long basin where people jog, skate and play pétanque along the quay. You pay for what you eat and drink, not for the seat.
linger:Le Pavillon des Canaux.why: Get there at opening on a weekday, claim the bathtub, and work until the lunch crowd arrives.
facts: Quai de la Loire, Bassin de la Villette, 19th
Tuesday to Sunday from 10:00; until midnight midweek, 1:00 Thursday to Saturday, 22:00 on Sunday (Oct 2026, listings differ)
Coffee and a slice of cake, or the weekend brunch
Yes by day, with Wi-Fi; some rooms ask you to close the laptop at meal times

linger:Ten Belles.name: Ten Belles
linger:Ten Belles.teaser: A 2012 counter by the Canal Saint-Martin, where the queue spills onto the pavement for a cortado
linger:Ten Belles.story: Ten Belles opened in 2012 a few steps from the Canal Saint-Martin, one of the first places in the city to pour specialty coffee with a proper sourdough loaf beside it. It began on Belleville Brûlerie beans (that roaster has its own card) and now roasts its own, and has grown to three Paris addresses. The original is still pocket-sized: a counter, a few stools, a kitchen at the back sending out pastries and lunch, and a line out the door at the weekend. The cortado is the drink people come back for; the bread is the reason to leave with something.
linger:Ten Belles.why: Take the coffee and a slice of bread to a bench by the locks; the room is too small to stay.
facts: 10 rue de la Grange-aux-Belles, 10th (métro Jacques Bonsergent)
Daily from about 8:30 on weekdays and 9:00 at weekends until late afternoon; listings differ, some show Monday closed
A cortado or flat white, and a loaf or a pastry
No: superb coffee, wrong room for a session. Café Craft is round the corner

linger:Café Craft.name: Café Craft
linger:Café Craft.teaser: Built from the start for people who came to work: long tables, a socket at every seat, Wi-Fi that holds
linger:Café Craft.story: Most Paris cafés tolerate a laptop at best. Café Craft, on the rue des Vinaigriers near the canal, was designed around it: long shared tables, a power socket within reach of every chair, solid Wi-Fi, and a room full of designers, coders and writers keeping their voices down. The coffee comes from Café Lomi, roasted in Paris, and the kitchen keeps a short list of salads, toasts and cakes going for people who are not leaving before evening. Its pricing has moved around over the years, from per-hour to per-cup, so read the board when you arrive.
linger:Café Craft.why: When you need a full afternoon of work near the canal and a café that wants you to stay, sit here.
facts: Monday to Saturday 9:00–19:00, Sunday from 10:00 (older listings; check)
A filter or flat white on Café Lomi beans, and lunch from the counter
Yes: sockets, Wi-Fi and long tables are the point of the place

around:Giverny.name: Giverny
around:Giverny.teaser: The lily pond and the green Japanese bridge, a hundred years after Monet died painting them
around:Giverny.story: Claude Monet rented the long pink house with green shutters in 1883 and spent the next forty-three years turning its land into a subject. In front of the house he laid the Clos Normand, a flower garden planted for colour like a palette; across the road he diverted a stream to make the water garden, with weeping willows, bamboo, the green Japanese footbridge and the water lilies he painted again and again until his death here in 1926. The gardeners still replant to his schemes every year. 2026 is the centenary of his death, and exhibitions in Paris and Normandy mark it.
around:Giverny.why: Book the first entry slot and go straight to the water garden before the crowds reach the bridge.
facts: Train from Paris Saint-Lazare to Vernon-Giverny, then the shuttle or a bike the last few kilometres; about 1h15 door to door
Half a day for the house and gardens; a full day with the Musée des impressionnismes in the village
The water garden and the Japanese bridge; the Clos Normand flower beds in front of the house
A picnic by the Seine at Vernon, or a lunch in the village; book ahead in May and June
1 April to 1 November 2026, 10:00–18:00, last entry 17:30; closed all winter

around:Auvers-sur-Oise.name: Auvers-sur-Oise
around:Auvers-sur-Oise.teaser: The village where Van Gogh painted some seventy canvases in seventy days, and the room where he died
around:Auvers-sur-Oise.story: Vincent van Gogh stepped off the train at Auvers in May 1890 and took a room in the attic of the Auberge Ravoux, an inn facing the town hall. In the seventy days before he died there, at the end of July, he painted about as many canvases: the church, the town hall, the thatched cottages, the wheatfields under storm clouds above the village. The attic room is about seven square metres and has been kept empty and as it was. Up the hill, past the church he painted, he lies in the cemetery against the wall beside his brother Theo, under a shared blanket of ivy.
around:Auvers-sur-Oise.why: Walk from the church up to the cemetery and on to the wheatfields beyond: you are standing in the paintings.
facts: Train from Paris Gare du Nord or Saint-Lazare with a change at Pontoise or Valmondois; about an hour
The attic room at the Auberge Ravoux; the church of Notre-Dame; the two graves in the cemetery
Lunch in the dining room of the Auberge Ravoux itself, if it is serving; the house and room are seasonal, so check dates before going

sources.label: Sortir à Paris: Heritage Days 2026, Auberge Ravoux

around:Fontainebleau & Barbizon.name: Fontainebleau & Barbizon
around:Fontainebleau & Barbizon.teaser: Sandstone boulders in an oak forest, a royal château at one edge and the painters' village at the other
around:Fontainebleau & Barbizon.story: The forest of Fontainebleau covers some 25,000 hectares of oak, pine, white sand and sandstone boulders an hour south of Paris. Climbers call it Font: the world's oldest bouldering ground, with thousands of numbered problems over soft sand, and the 'Font' grading scale that climbers everywhere now use. In the 1830s the same light and rock drew Millet, Théodore Rousseau and Corot out of their studios to paint trees and peasants outdoors, a generation before the Impressionists. Their village, Barbizon, is still one street of stone houses, with the Auberge Ganne where they lodged and painted on the furniture, and the houses of Millet and Rousseau.
around:Fontainebleau & Barbizon.why: Spend the morning on the rocks at Trois Pignons or Bas-Bréau, then end the day in Barbizon's single street.
facts: Train from Paris Gare de Lyon to Fontainebleau-Avon, then bus to the château; the forest sites and Barbizon need a car, taxi or bike
A full day for the forest and Barbizon; add half a day for the château
The boulders and sand of Trois Pignons; the Auberge Ganne and the Millet house in Barbizon; the château of Fontainebleau (€17, closed Tuesday, Oct 2026)
A picnic among the rocks, or lunch in Barbizon's main street
Soft shoes and a brush mat if you climb; water, as there are no taps in the forest

around:Versailles.name: Versailles
around:Versailles.teaser: The palace, the gardens, the Trianons, and the king's kitchen garden still worked by students
around:Versailles.story: Louis XIV turned his father's hunting lodge into the seat of government and moved the court here in 1682; the Hall of Mirrors, the State Apartments and the gardens laid out by Le Nôtre are the result. Allow the whole day: the palace in the morning, then the long walk down the Grand Canal to the Trianons and Marie-Antoinette's hamlet. For a cook, the best stop is outside the gates: the Potager du Roi, the king's kitchen garden laid out from 1678 by Jean-Baptiste de La Quintinie, its walled squares of espaliered pears and apples and vegetable beds still tended by the École nationale supérieure de paysage.
around:Versailles.why: Finish at the Potager du Roi, walled, quiet and cheap, where the fruit trees are still trained as they were for the king.
facts: RER C to Versailles Château Rive Gauche; or train from Saint-Lazare to Versailles Rive Droite, or from Montparnasse to Versailles Chantiers; about 40 minutes
The Hall of Mirrors at opening; the gardens and the Trianons; the Potager du Roi (Tuesday to Sunday 10:00–18:00; €8 April to October, €5 November and December, Oct 2026)
A picnic in the park, or the covered market at Notre-Dame in town
Palace closed Monday; timed entry, booked online even for free visitors
Passport (whole estate) €25 low season, €35 high season; €22/€32 for France and EEA residents (Oct 2026)

around:Vaux-le-Vicomte.name: Vaux-le-Vicomte
around:Vaux-le-Vicomte.teaser: The château so beautiful it got its owner arrested, built by the team Louis XIV then took for Versailles
around:Vaux-le-Vicomte.story: Nicolas Fouquet, Louis XIV's finance minister, brought together the architect Louis Le Vau, the painter Charles Le Brun and the gardener André Le Nôtre to build Vaux, the first time the three worked as one. On 17 August 1661 he threw a fête for the young king, with fountains, a Molière comedy and fireworks. Three weeks later Fouquet was arrested, and he died in prison. The king took the three men, the ideas and even orange trees to Versailles. Vaux, privately owned and still lived in, is smaller, more unified, far quieter, and its gardens, with their false perspectives, are pure Le Nôtre.
around:Vaux-le-Vicomte.why: Walk to the far end of the gardens and look back: the ground drops and rises in ways you could not see from the house.
facts: Train from Paris Gare de Lyon to Melun, then the Châteaubus shuttle; about 1 hour
Half a day to a full day
The view from the dome; the gardens' hidden canal; the Grand Noël, 14 November 2026 to 3 January 2027, booking required
The estate's restaurant or a picnic outside the gardens
The 2026 season opened 14 March; the summer candlelit Saturdays ended 26 September; check the late-autumn dates
About €22 château and gardens, €16 gardens only (Oct 2026)

around:Chantilly.name: Chantilly
around:Chantilly.teaser: A château on its own lake, a picture gallery frozen by a will, and a palace built for horses
around:Chantilly.story: The Château de Chantilly rises from a lake of its own north of Paris. Its last private owner, Henri d'Orléans, duc d'Aumale, left it with his collection to the Institut de France on one condition: nothing may be lent, sold or moved. So the Musée Condé still hangs its old masters as he arranged them, floor to ceiling, and after the Louvre it is often called the richest picture collection in France. Across the lawn, the Grandes Écuries, the great stables, are so grand they are mistaken for the château, and still house horses and a riding show. The town claims crème Chantilly; the story is told, not proved.
around:Chantilly.why: See the paintings hung in the duke's order, then catch the horses in the Grandes Écuries dome.
facts: Train from Paris Gare du Nord to Chantilly-Gouvieux, then a walk or shuttle; about 40 minutes
The Musée Condé galleries; the Grandes Écuries and the equestrian show; the gardens by Le Nôtre
Crème Chantilly on anything, at the estate's restaurant
Closed Tuesday; 10:00–18:00 in high season, shorter hours in winter

around:Provins.name: Provins
around:Provins.teaser: Medieval ramparts, a 12th-century keep and the rose of Provins, an hour and a half by train
around:Provins.story: In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries the counts of Champagne made Provins one of the great fair towns of Europe, where merchants from Flanders and Italy traded cloth and spices under the counts' protection. When the trade moved on, the town shrank and was not rebuilt, so it survived largely as it was, which is why UNESCO listed it. You can walk more than a kilometre of the ramparts, climb the Tour César keep, and go down into the underground galleries cut under the upper town. The red rose, Rosa gallica, is everywhere in jam, honey and sweets; the story that Thibaut IV brought it back from crusade is legend.
around:Provins.why: Walk the ramparts from the Porte Saint-Jean, then buy rose-petal jam on the way to the station.
facts: Transilien line P from Paris Gare de l'Est, direct, about 1h25
The ramparts and the Porte Saint-Jean; the Tour César; the underground galleries
Lunch in the upper town, with something made of rose to finish

around:Guinguette de l'Ile du Martin-Pec.name: Guinguette de l'Île du Martin-Pêcheur
around:Guinguette de l'Ile du Martin-Pec.teaser: Over a footbridge to a Marne island, for a drink under the trees where Parisians once danced on Sundays
around:Guinguette de l'Ile du Martin-Pec.story: From the late nineteenth century, Parisians took the train to the banks of the Marne on Sundays to eat fried fish, drink white wine and dance to the accordion in the open-air guinguettes, the world the Impressionists painted. Almost all of them have gone. On a small island at Champigny-sur-Marne, one was revived in 1993: you cross a footbridge to a big terrace under the trees, with a pétanque pitch and the river all round. A new team has run it since 2023, with pizzas, sharing plates, cocktails and a Sunday brunch, so the old accordion afternoons are no longer the whole programme. Check what is on before you go.
around:Guinguette de l'Ile du Martin-Pec.why: Come on a warm weekend afternoon, cross the footbridge, and order something cold on the river terrace.
facts: RER A to Champigny, then about 7 minutes on foot over the Pont de Champigny and left along the quai
The crossing to the island and the terrace on the water
Sharing plates and pizzas at the guinguette; Sunday brunch
Seasonal, to 1 November in 2026; evenings midweek and from noon at weekends (listings differ)
